blocks.text: [III, 2] Hence the same Pomarius, who above wrote אבל לפי קמחי הוא חולי שיוליד דקות הגוף ואבודו, But according to Kimchi it is a disease producing wasting of the body and its destruction. And Aquinas: חולי מה שגורם כיחוש ודלות לגוף עד שמאבדו והוא מן קדחא, It is a disease which causes leanness and wasting of the body, until it consumes it entirely; and this comes from fever. Everyone can see that these words describe phthisis, or consumption. And indeed the Arabic سحاف [suḥāf] sochaph in Giauhari [col. 264] is the same as سل [sill] sil. That this word signifies phthisis is taught, among others, by Avicenna in the treatise On Phthisis, book 3, Fen 10, tract. 4, ch. 18. Moreover, the Hebrew שחפת sachepheth and the Arabic سحاف [suḥāf] sochaph have the same radicals, except that the Arabs, as is their custom, change the Hebrew Shin into Sin. So the two words certainly signify the same disease. Accordingly, in Moses, for שחפת the Arabs have السل [al-sill] phthisis, or حمي السل [ḥummā al-sill], phthisical fever. I also suspect that the Greeks rendered it ἀτροφίαν [atrophian], which is among the species of phthisis, although our copies have shown ἀπορίαν [aporian] for many centuries now. For so Jerome read, and accordingly he interprets שחפת as poverty. However that may be, that שחפת is not ἀπορίαν [aporian], poverty, is clear from the fact that in both passages of the Law it is counted among the kinds of diseases. Therefore שחפת is a disease, and indeed the one we have named: namely phthisis, or consumption. This is confirmed from the Talmudists, among whom שחוף means consumptive, as the distinguished Buxtorf proves from Sota fol. 26 b. Moreover, among other Hebrew writers שחף in Kal is to waste away, in Niphal to become consumptive, in Piel to cause to waste away, as the same author affirms. It is therefore probable that שחף sachaph is a bird named from wasting, and that Jerome, following the Greeks, rightly rendered it larus [gull] (that is, French movette). Of this bird Belon, book 3, chapter 13, says: No bird is so light in proportion to its bulk. For though it is bigger than a hen, it has not as much flesh as a quail. This is found above all in the cepphus, a very light species of gull, which has a great deal of plumage but very little flesh. The Scholiast on Aristophanes, on the Peace: Εὔηθες ζῶον ὁ κέπφος, etc. Ἐκ δὲ τῆς θαλάττης ζῆν αὐτὸν λέγουσιν, ἐσθίοντα τὸν ἀφρόν· εἶναι δὲ αὐτὸν πολὺν μὲν ἐν τοῖς πτεροῖς, ὀλίγον δὲ ἐν τοῖς κρέασι [Euēthes zōon ho kepphos, etc. Ek de tēs thalattēs zēn auton legousin, esthionta ton aphron; einai de auton polyn men en tois pterois, oligon de en tois kreasi]. The cepphus is a stupid animal, etc. They say that it lives from the sea, eating the foam, and that it has much plumage but little flesh. Hence Hesychius: Κέπφος· εἶδος ὀρνέου κουφοτάτου, περὶ τὴν θάλασσαν διατρίβοντος, ὃ εὐχερῶς ὑπὸ ἀνέμου μετάγεται [Kepphos; eidos orneou kouphotatou, peri tēn thalassan diatribontos, ho eucherōs hypo anemou metagetai]. Cepphus: a species of very light bird, accustomed to spend its time about the sea, which is easily carried off by the wind. And Suidas: Κέπφος· εἶδος ὀρνέου ὁ λεγόμενος λάρος· ἔστι δὲ κοῦφον, καὶ ἐπιπλέον τοῖς κύμασιν [Kepphos; eidos orneou ho legomenos laros; esti de kouphon, kai epipleon tois kymasin]; Cepphus: a species of bird, which is also called larus; it is light, and floats on the waves. His statement that it is called by another name larus comes from the Scholiast on Aristophanes, on the Plutus, whose words on the cepphus are: Καλεῖται δὲ κοινῶς λάρος [Kaleitai de koinōs laros]. It is commonly called larus. Accordingly they are joined as synonyms in the proverb Κέπφος λάρος [Kepphos laros] in Erasmus and others. And in Hesychius, Κὴξ [Kēx] for Apion is ὁ λάρος [ho laros], but others render it κέπφον [kephon], [III, 3] and others again ἐφυϊάν [ephyian]; read αἰθυϊὰν [aithyian], that is, diver. Yet you may gather that the gull and the cepphus differ from these words of Aristotle, History, book 8, chapter 3: Περὶ δὲ τὴν θάλατταν καὶ ἀλκύων, καὶ κήρυλος, etc. Ἔτι δὲ ὁ λάρος ὁ λευκὸς, καὶ κέπφος, καὶ χαράδριος [Peri de tēn thalattan kai alkyōn, kai kērylos, etc. Eti de ho laros ho leukos, kai kepphos, kai charadrios]; But about the sea there are also the alcyon and the cerylus, etc. Also the white gull, and the cepphus, and the charadrius. The cepphus and the gull, then, are not entirely the same, but very similar birds. Hence the Scholiast on Nicander, on the Alexipharmaca: Ὁ δὲ κέπφος θαλάσσιόν ἐστι ὄρνεον παραπλήσιον λάρῳ [Ho de kepphos thalassion esti orneon paraplēsion larō]. Gesner thinks they are birds of the same genus, or that the cepphus is a species of gull. However the matter stands, the name שחף suits both the gull and the cepphus exceedingly well, since both birds are described as almost devoid of flesh, as if consumed by wasting ^{(1)}.
